btos.label: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21)

name: Mining
blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

summary: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling are the established deployments in a sector that adopted automation early. Mining AI splits into two horizons: exploration - long-term forecasting from satellite, magnetic, and core-scan data toward drilling targets - and site operations, where sensor streams and telemetry drive machinery, maintenance, and safety minute by minute.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey records that 7.2% of firms in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction reported using AI in the most recent measurement period, down from 7.9% in the prior period. Those figures come directly from businesses answering whether they used AI in the previous two weeks, making this one of the few sectors where adoption is measured rather than estimated. The modest headline share does not capture the outsized operational role AI already plays at the largest operators, where scale makes even incremental efficiency gains consequential.

On the operations side, Komatsu, one of the two dominant mining-equipment manufacturers, has moved autonomous haulage and fleet management into mainstream commercial offerings, and has entered a strategic partnership with AIM Intelligent Machines for autonomous operation of bulldozers and hydraulic excavators. That makes AI-driven equipment a purchasable product rather than a bespoke experiment. Rio Tinto's automation program, running autonomous haul trucks and drills at scale, represents the primary-source record of what day-to-day operational AI looks like in production mining. Freeport-McMoRan applies machine-learning models to processing, with the stated aim of maximizing mill throughput and ore recovery at existing operations. Newmont uses AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring.

At the exploration end, KoBold Metals applies machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits including copper, cobalt, lithium, and nickel, and is developing the Mingomba project in Zambia, described as one of the world's largest copper mines. GeologicAI offers computer-vision core scanning, combining RGB, XRF, hyperspectral, and LiDAR sensors to produce what it describes as the most accurate and consistent datasets in the industry, and counts Agnico Eagle among its clients. The USGS Mineral Resources Program and its Earth Mapping Resources Initiative are systematically re-mapping US geology with modern geophysics, generating the satellite, geophysical, and historical datasets that exploration machine-learning models train on, making federal data infrastructure a quiet enabler of private AI prospectivity work.

The International Council on Mining and Metals tracks ESG standards, automated safety monitoring, and digital transformation across major international operators, and publishes annual safety data on fatalities, injuries, and workplace hazards. Its 2025 safety report and ongoing tailings management work reflect the sector's dual pressure: improve safety records while managing environmental obligations. The National Mining Association serves as the US policy voice, navigating regulatory change and technology adoption questions before Congress and federal agencies. The Society for Mining, Metallurgy and Exploration publishes the working-group research that underpins technical decisions around AI and automation in mineral processing.

For a reader weighing deployment, the clearest takeaways from what these sources collectively show are that AI in mining concentrates in two distinct layers: processing optimization and predictive maintenance at operating mines, and geospatial modelling and core analysis at the exploration stage. Equipment vendors like Komatsu have commoditized parts of the autonomous haulage stack, lowering the barrier for operators who do not want to build internally. Specialist vendors like GeologicAI address the geology-as-data problem that exploration AI requires. The sector's regulatory complexity, documented by the NMA and ICMM, means that AI deployment decisions rarely happen in isolation from permitting, safety, and environmental reporting obligations, and organizations active in those policy spaces are worth monitoring for signals about where friction will emerge.
